title: Comets probably didn’t deliver life’s building blocks to Earth

sections.title: Conversation 1
sections.scene: Two students discuss a public lecture on the origins of life and plan a follow-up seminar.

script.en: Did you go to Dr. Patel's lecture last night on how life began on Earth?
I did, and I have to say it was not what I expected. I thought we would hear mostly about the famous Miller-Urey experiment, but she spent nearly half the talk on comets.
Right, she argued that the old picture of comets as delivery trucks for organic molecules is looking weaker than most textbooks suggest.
That was the part that surprised me. She kept saying that even if a comet carries the right chemicals, getting them to the surface intact is a completely different problem.
And she showed those computer models about hydrogen cyanide. I had never thought about how fast and at what angle a comet would have to strike for anything to survive.
The numbers were striking. If I remember correctly, she said only about one impact in a billion years might have delivered a meaningful amount.
That is what I wrote down too. But she was careful to say the study does not completely rule out comets. It just makes them a much less likely source.

Which leaves asteroids, volcanoes and deep-sea vents as alternatives. I found the asteroid idea the most convincing, because those carbon-rich rocks seem to have a better chance of arriving in one piece.
I am thinking of proposing a seminar on this for our astronomy club. Would you be willing to present the comet argument while I cover the asteroid side?
I would, but only if we keep the focus on evidence rather than on who tells the better story. The topic attracts a lot of speculation.
Agreed. Let us meet tomorrow to sketch out the structure and decide which studies to assign as reading.
Fine. I will bring the lecture handout and a couple of review articles I found this morning.

script.en: For decades, one of the most attractive ideas in the study of life's origins has been that comets delivered the necessary chemicals to the young Earth. The picture is simple and appealing: icy bodies rich in carbon and nitrogen collide with the planet, and their cargo seeds the first steps toward biology. A recent modeling study, however, suggests that this picture deserves a second look. The researchers focused on hydrogen cyanide, a molecule that is unusually stable and that can release energy to drive later reactions. If even this robust compound struggles to survive an impact, they reasoned, more fragile molecules would fare worse. Their simulations tracked comets passing through the modern atmosphere and striking the surface, and they also considered the denser early atmosphere, which would have been even more destructive. The results were sobering. On average, only about one impact over more than a billion years would have delivered a meaningful amount of hydrogen cyanide. To survive at all, a comet would need to be larger than one hundred meters across, to move slowly and to arrive at a shallow angle. It would also have to hit land rather than ocean, because water would dilute the chemicals too quickly to trigger useful reactions. The study does not close the case. It leaves open the possibility that a rare comet did contribute, and it notes that Mars, with its thinner atmosphere and weaker gravity, may have received carbon-based molecules more easily. But it does shift attention toward other candidates, including carbon-rich asteroids, volcanoes and hydrothermal vents. For students of science, the episode offers a useful lesson. A familiar story can survive for years not because the evidence is strong but because it is easy to repeat. When new tools allow researchers to test that story, the result may be less a dramatic refutation than a quiet redistribution of probability. That is how scientific understanding usually advances.

sections.title: Comets Probably Didn't Deliver Life's Building Blocks to Earth
sections.passage:
For decades, the idea that comets seeded the young Earth with the chemicals needed for life has been repeated in textbooks and documentaries. A new modeling study, published October 28 in Scientific Reports, challenges that familiar story. The researchers do not claim to have disproved it entirely, but they argue that the delivery scenario is far less plausible than commonly assumed.

The study centers on hydrogen cyanide, a molecule containing carbon and nitrogen that is left over from the solar system's formation. Its strong internal bond allows it to release energy that can drive later reactions, and this same bond makes it unusually stable compared with other carbon-based compounds. The team reasoned that if even this robust molecule struggles to survive an impact, more fragile chemicals would fare worse.

Using computer simulations, the researchers estimated how often hydrogen cyanide would remain intact as a comet passed through Earth's atmosphere and struck the surface. They also considered the early atmosphere, which was probably denser and therefore even more destructive. The results were sobering: on average, only about one impact over more than a billion years would have delivered a meaningful amount. To survive, a comet would need to be larger than one hundred meters across, to move slowly and to arrive at a shallow angle. It would also have to hit land rather than ocean, since water would dilute the chemicals too quickly to trigger useful reactions.

The study does not close the case. It leaves open the possibility that a rare comet did contribute, and it suggests that Mars, with its thinner atmosphere and weaker gravity, may have received carbon-based molecules more easily. But it does shift attention toward other candidates, including carbon-rich asteroids known as carbonaceous chondrites, as well as volcanoes and hydrothermal vents.

Outside researchers have responded with cautious interest. Nicolle Zellner, a physicist not involved in the work, says it is important to revisit old ideas as understanding of comets and the early solar system improves. Gordon Osinski, a planetary geologist, predicts that the study will make people think twice about comets as the originator of organics and hopes others will try to reproduce the results.

For students of science, the episode offers a useful lesson. A familiar story can survive for years not because the evidence is strong but because it is easy to repeat. When new tools allow researchers to test that story, the outcome may be less a dramatic refutation than a quiet redistribution of probability. That is how scientific understanding usually advances.

long_sentences.en: “Even though we see that comets contain all of these molecules in really high concentrations, it’s not straightforward to go from there to saying we’re going to have all of these available for prebiotic chemistry on the surface of the Earth,” says Richard Anslow, a planetary scientist at the Met Office, the national meteorological service for the United Kingdom in Exeter.

“So if things look bad for hydrogen cyanide, then we think it’s going to be much harder for other, more complicated molecules that are more likely to be broken down during these impacts.” Based on the simulations, a comet impact that kept hydrogen cyanide intact would be extremely unlikely, the team found.

If Earth’s carbon-based chemicals didn’t come from comets, they may have come from carbon-rich asteroids called carbonaceous chondrites , says Gordon Osinski, a planetary geologist at Western University in London, Canada, who was not involved in the study.
